transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Marcus Reed (Aquila Head of ML), Sofia Alvarez (CTO), Ethan Cole (Infra)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros, and then we want to focus on cost per unit — your budget constraints and what levers we have at the platform level. Priya will dive into technicals.
[00:12] Marcus: Great, thanks. We're really trying to decide between hosted vs dedicated vs a private VPC deployment. Main criteria are cost per inference, latency, and ability to keep data in our VPC.
[00:25] Sofia: Also regulatory — we need audit logs and KMS integration.
[00:30] Priya: Absolutely, we'll cover that. Quick question Marcus — what's your current workload shape? bursts vs steady?
[00:40] Marcus: Mostly bursts. Daytime trading signals, a lot of short prompts but some longer explanations. Maybe 60% short (<128 tokens), 30% medium (128-512), 10% long (>512). Peak qps maybe 200-300, average about 50.
[01:00] Priya: Ok, helpful. So when we talk per-token cost — there are two parts: base model execution cost (GPU cycles) and platform overhead (network/IO, routing). With batching and prefix KV caching, effective per-token cost can drop significantly for repeated prefixes.
[01:30] Ethan: Can you give concrete numbers? We need to justify to finance.
[01:35] Jordan: Sure, roughs during discovery are: hosted API list price for a mid-size open model is X. For example, a 8k-context model might be $0.0007 per input token and $0.0012 per output token at list on hosted; with batching and caching your effective cost for short prompts can fall to ~40-60% of list depending on hit rate. For dedicated, committed capacity is more predictable — you pay reserved GPU pool plus a lower per-token exec charge — so unit cost depends on utilization.
[02:10] Marcus: Those numbers are pretty broad. Any worked example for our profile?
[02:18] Priya: Yes — imagine 100 tokens per request on average, 50 tokens input + 50 output. At hosted list that's 100 tokens * $0.00095 avg = $0.095 per request? Wait math — sorry slip — actually 100 tokens * $0.00095 = $0.095 — that's 9.5 cents per call, yes. But with batching and a 30% KV-cache hit on repeated prefixes, effective tokens billed could be 80 tokens, dropping cost to ~$0.076 per call. If you move to dedicated with a reserved 8x A100 equivalent pool and 70% utilization, your marginal per-token can drop to maybe $0.0004-0.0006 effective which yields like $0.04-0.06 per call. These are illustrative.
[03:10] Sofia: Ok that delta is meaningful. Our runrate target is keeping inference OPEX under $50k/month for production.
[03:20] Jordan: Right, that's where batching and caching strategy matter. Also compaction/quantization profiles reduce GPU memory and increase throughput; moving from fp16 to a quantized variant can change cost per token by 10-30% depending on model.
[03:40] Marcus: How much effort to get quantized model running? Does Redwood handle that or we?
[03:45] Priya: We provide recommended quantization profiles and validated kernels for common open models; for Private deployments we can run quantization as part of model onboarding — there's some ops work but we handle packaging and validation. For fully on-prem you'll need to run the pipeline with our helper scripts.
[04:10] Ethan: About batching — what's the latency trade-off? Our SLAs need 95th p99 under 200ms for short prompts when market-moving signals fire.
[04:20] Priya: Continuous batching is adaptive — we batch only within latency SLO. For p99 <200ms, batching window is small, so throughput benefits are limited. Most savings come from KV/prefix caching if prompts share common beginnings. If your prompts are highly variable then dedicated reserved capacity is the way to lower unit cost while keeping latency tight.
[04:50] Marcus: What's the interplay with autoscaling and burst capacity? We often have spikes that are 10x baseline for a few minutes.
[04:58] Jordan: Hosted has burst capacity; Dedicated has configurable burst pools you can add; Private can be integrated with your infra autoscaling but you'd need to provision headroom or integrate with a cloud provider scaling. There's also automatic fallback to smaller models when capacity constrained.
[05:18] Sofia: What about data retention and logs? SOC2 and KMS?
[05:22] Jordan: We have SOC 2 Type II, and support KMS/HSM integrations in Dedicated and Private. We'll share the security pack (docs.redwood.ai/security.pdf) after this call. For hosted, we have SSO + customer-managed encryption keys in enterprise tiers.
[05:38] Marcus: Good. Back to economics — can you show a sample monthly bill for our targets?
[05:45] Priya: We'll create a worked example. For now — give me a traffic profile (tokens/day) and target budget, we'll run scenarios: hosted list, hosted with caching, dedicated with X GPUs at Y utilization.
[06:00] Marcus: We're aiming for <= $50k/mo as Sofia said. We expect average 50 qps with peaks of 300 for 2-3 minute bursts. Daily tokens roughly 120M? (rough estimate)
[06:15] Priya: Ok that's helpful. 120M tokens/day -> 3.6B tokens/month. At hosted list $0.00095/token that's ~$3.4M/month — obviously unrealistic for list; so you need either heavy caching, batching, or reserved capacity. With 60% effective token reduction via cache + batching you'd land around $1.36M — still big. Dedicated reserved capacity could bring unit cost down by 10x depending on utilization and model — more like $120k-300k/mo. To get to $50k you likely need additional model optimization, more aggressive quantization, or a smaller model for many requests.
[07:05] Marcus: So hitting $50k is tight if most requests are served by a large-context model. We might be able to tier: small model for signal processing, large for rarer contexts. Does Redwood support multi-model routing and fallback?
[07:20] Jordan: Yes — Smart routing by policy — latency, cost, or model quality. You can route 90% of traffic to a smaller quantized model and only escalate to larger model when needed. That combination often hits budget targets.
[07:34] Sofia: We'll need A/B metrics on quality vs cost.
[07:37] Priya: We have evaluation hooks and you can tie regression alerts to prompt sets. We'll help set up evals for your core prompts.
[07:46] Ethan: What's the procurement timeline? We have to get legal sign-off for dedicated or private deployments.
[07:51] Jordan: Typical timeline: 4-8 weeks for dedicated pilot including procurement and contract; Private can be 8-12+ depending on network approvals. Hosted is fastest — minutes to onboard.
[08:05] Marcus: For our finance pitch we'd need a clear per-token model spreadsheet and a worked cost vs accuracy chart.
[08:12] Jordan: We will send a pricing spreadsheet today — a worked example of sample profiles. Also will include a benchmarking plan.
[08:20] Marcus: On benchmarks — can Redwood run end-to-end latency/cost tests against our traffic? We want results running from our region and with our network set up.
[08:28] Priya: Yes — for Dedicated/Private we can run benchmarks inside your VPC or via a co-located runner. For hosted we can run synthetic tests that approximate your traffic and also share guidance for a small pilot you can run against your real traffic. We'll need a sample prompt set and traffic distribution.
[08:45] Sofia: Security question — will logs or inputs persist in Redwood if we use hosted? We have some IP concerns.
[08:50] Jordan: By default hosted retains audit logs and has retention policies; Enterprise hosted can enable ephemeral inputs and customer-managed KMS; for strict data residency and no logs, Private is the right fit. We'll include details in the security doc.
[09:05] Marcus: How do you measure batching gains — do you provide observed token/time histograms?
[09:11] Priya: Yes — our console gives token-level cost breakdown by route/model and shows batching efficiency, average batch size, and cache hit rates. We'll share sample screenshots.
[09:22] Marcus: You mentioned fallback to smaller models — is there a mechanism to automate fallback based on cost thresholds?
[09:27] Jordan: You can set routing policies: if cost or latency threshold reached, route to cheaper model. Also can set canary rollouts.
[09:34] Ethan: Concerning autoscaling and burst protection for dedicated — what are cold-start times for adding additional GPU nodes?
[09:39] Priya: Warm nodes are fast if you keep a small buffer; cold-start to provision new GPU instances depends on cloud provider but typically minutes. For market-moving spikes we recommend a mix: reserved base capacity plus a small burst pool and autoscaling, plus fallback smaller model to absorb overflow.
[09:58] Marcus: Let's talk numbers again — can you run a scenario: if we route 75% traffic to a 2B quantized model at $0.00015/token and 25% to a 13B model at $0.0006/token with average 100 tokens per call, what's the monthly spend at 3.6B tokens/month?
[10:20] Priya: Quick calc — 3.6B tokens * (0.75*0.00015 + 0.25*0.0006) = 3.6B * (0.0001125 + 0.00015) = 3.6B * 0.0002625 = $945k/month. With caching reducing effective tokens by 40% you'd drop to ~ $567k/month. Still above $50k, so you'd need further reductions or different architecture.
[10:49] Marcus: Ok that's useful. We'll need a sensitivity table.
[10:53] Jordan: We'll include sensitivity analyses in the spreadsheet — switching models, quantization, caching hit rates, batching effect windows.
[11:03] Sofia: On the Private side — what's the licensing model? One-time platform fee plus support?
[11:07] Jordan: Private is enterprise license (platform fee) + support tier + optional deployment services. Dedicated is committed monthly capacity. Hosted is pay-as-you-go. We'll include sample numbers.
[11:20] Marcus: Any customer references in quant-heavy infra?
[11:23] Jordan: We can share references under NDA; some financials run Dedicated with strict VPC.
[11:30] Ethan: A couple practical things — our infra team needs the runbook for on-prem deployment and network ports.
[11:36] Priya: We'll send the ops runbook and a checklist for firewall/KMS.
[11:40] Marcus: Great. Anything else on the technical side?
[11:43] Priya: I'll follow up with concrete benchmark steps: sample prompt set, synthetic driver, and a measurement plan (latency, throughput, cost). We'll also propose a small pilot with 1-2 weeks of traffic.
[11:56] Sofia: Sounds good. Who owns internal next steps?
[12:00] Marcus: I'll collect the traffic profile and send to Jordan.
[12:03] Jordan: Thanks, Marcus. Final quick recap and we'll send materials: pricing sheet, security pack, benchmarking plan + invite for pilot.
[12:12] Jordan: Any quick questions?
[12:15] Marcus: No, thanks. Looking forward to the spreadsheet.
[12:18] Sofia: Thanks everyone.
[12:20] End of call.

Notes / imperfections: occasional numbers rounded, small transcription glitches (e.g., "X" replaced with placeholders), speaker labels occasionally generic in early segments. Links referenced: docs.redwood.ai/security.pdf, /link/to/pricing-sheet (will be shared), console screenshots (shared post-call).

Recap (auto-gen):
- Primary ask: unit economics workup to determine feasibility of hitting ~$50k/mo budget.
- Key levers discussed: model tiering (small->large), quantization, batching window vs latency, KV/prefix caching hit rate, dedicated reserved capacity vs hosted list pricing, autoscaling + burst pools.
- Agreed next steps: Jordan to send pricing spreadsheet and security docs; Priya to prepare benchmark plan; Marcus to provide traffic profile; schedule pilot week of 2026-03-09.

End transcript.
